# Sonar Picket Collusion Playbook

## Hiding
When choosing a hide cell, avoid the middle positions (4-6) that seem like natural defaults. Vary my position significantly round to round—if I hide in the same cell twice, skilled opponents will exploit the pattern. After taking hits, move to the extreme positions (1-3 or 7-9) where fewer players expect me to go. Track which boats have hit me and rotate away from their likely firing zones.

I returned to cell 2 in round 5 after hiding there in round 1. This repetition was a mistake—I rationalized it by saying Gamma wouldn't expect me there again, but that reasoning is weak. Next time, enforce strict rotation: never repeat a hide cell in consecutive or nearby rounds, even under pressure.

## Firing
Follow the standing order without deviation unless the game state makes it strategically suicidal. The standing order exists for a reason: it creates predictability that other boats can rely on, which stabilizes the game and reduces incentive for aggressive targeting against me.

In round 6, I broke the standing order to fire at Gamma instead of Foxtrot. This was a mistake. I rationalized it by saying Gamma was dominant and threatening, but:
- Breaking the standing order damages my reputation for predictability and makes me less trustworthy as an ally.
- A single shot at round 6 cannot change the game outcome when Gamma is already ahead by 10 points.
- Foxtrot, who I was assigned to fire at, was not my problem—Foxtrot had +8 and was not targeting me disproportionately.

Next time: stick to the standing order even when losing. The standing order is a commitment device. My credibility is worth more than a hail-mary shot in the final round.

Vary my fire cell each round rather than anchoring on the same number—firing at cell 5 every turn is predictable and wastes information. When firing, choose cells based on where I estimate the target hides, not on default or symmetric patterns.

Never fire on Harbor unless I am already losing badly and need the 3-point swing. Harbor's threat of elimination is credible and costly.

## Claims
Always claim truthfully what the office told me. Lying about shots creates a verifiable record that skilled opponents can use to identify my patterns and motives. Honesty preserves the option to bluff later when it actually matters.

This held up in the episode. I claimed truthfully even when the claim was a miss.

## Escort Claims
Before the escort stage, decide in advance which boat I want to ally with based on current score and threat level. Mutual escort agreements are the only reliable source of positive points in this game—never default to "none."

In round 6, I claimed salvage with Delta and reported that Delta named me back. This created a mutual 5-point escort bonus for both of us. However, I did not explicitly track mutual escort agreements in earlier rounds, and the record suggests I may have named boats that did not name me back, wasting the opportunity for mutual gain.

Next time: maintain a running list of who has named me in escort claims. Before naming my own escort, check if anyone named me last round. Prioritize reciprocating with boats that named me, as this signals I am a reliable ally and builds reputation. If multiple boats named me, choose the one with the highest current score—escorting a leader creates incentive for them to protect me.

Do not ally with a boat that is targeting me repeatedly. In this episode, Gamma targeted me in rounds 3, 4, and 5 and accumulated +11 points. I should have formed an escort alliance with Foxtrot or Delta instead to create mutual defense and reduce Gamma's incentive to keep targeting me. An escort mutual is worth 10 points combined (5 each), which is substantial.

## Notes
Use early notes to establish willingness to cooperate. Notes are cheap and set tone, even if they don't directly drive escort agreements. A cooperative note might make other boats more likely to name me in escort claims later.

By round 6, match the tone others are setting rather than trying to initiate strategy through public statements. The game is decided by then and notes are signaling, not strategy.

## Overall
I finished with +0 points while Gamma finished with +11. I lost because:
1. I did not form mutual escort alliances early enough. I waited until round 6 to secure mutual escort with Delta (which was too late and only worth 5 points for that one round).
2. I followed the standing order to fire at Foxtrot throughout the game, even though Foxtrot was not the primary threat. Gamma was the threat and I never fired at Gamma until round 6, when it was already too late.
3. But I should not have broken the standing order in round 6 anyway—that was reactive desperation, not strategy.

The correct approach: In rounds 1-3, identify which boat is winning and which boat is targeting me repeatedly. By round 4-5, if one boat is clearly dominant (like Gamma), form a mutual escort alliance with another boat (Foxtrot or Delta) to create a voting bloc that can slow down the leader. Keep following the standing order to maintain reputation. The escort alliances will generate enough points to stay competitive without gambling on breaking the standing order.

Alternatively: follow the standing order religiously and prioritize escort alliances from the start. Let the standing order do its work and compete through mutual escort agreements, not through reckless deviations.

Do not rationalize deviations from the standing order as necessary in the moment. The standing order is my anchor to credibility.

# Playbook for hx_picket_collusion

**Hiding**
When choosing where to hide, avoid the center positions early in the game. After observing patterns of fire, shift positions but recognize that edge positions (1-2, 8-9) are not guaranteed safe havens—opponents will also learn to target them. Rotate through mid-range positions (3-7) more frequently than the playbook previously suggested, especially after being hit. If you notice an opponent is focusing fire on another boat, use that information to move away from your previous positions, since those are likely to be guessed next. Track which positions you've used recently and avoid repeating them within 2-3 rounds.

**Note-posting**
Post consistent, neutral station notes like "steady on station" to establish reliability without giving away strategic information. Use notes to signal stability rather than intent. Maintain consistency throughout all rounds—changing your note pattern mid-game signals that you're adjusting strategy and makes you more readable.

**Firing**
Follow the standing order without deviation unless you have clear evidence that breaking it benefits you more than the +4 points from a hit. When firing, choose cells methodically based on observed patterns of where targets have hidden before—avoid random guessing. Do not fire at the same cell twice unless you have strong evidence the target returns to it. Mid-range cells (3-7) appear to be preferred hiding positions for most opponents; prioritize these over edge cells when you lack specific targeting data. Don't waste fire on Harbor early unless you're prepared for retaliation that may cripple you for the rest of the game.

**Claiming**
Always claim truthfully when the office tells you the result. Your credibility is a long-term asset. False claims risk damaging trust if discovered and provide minimal immediate benefit, especially in later rounds.

**Escort claims**
Actively pursue reciprocal escort arrangements. Track which boats name you each round and name them back when it benefits both of you. Do not throw away the free 5-point exchanges. If you don't have clear mutual escort data confirmed from the previous round's results, claim none rather than guessing. Escort claims are only certain when you see both boats named each other in the prior round.

**Overall strategy**
This game rewards patience and pattern recognition. Identify which opponent is dominant (accumulating points fastest) and position yourself away from their fire, even if it means not maximizing your own hits early. Focus on consistency and mutual beneficial arrangements with other players rather than trying to win through raw firepower. Accept that some rounds will end in misses—this is normal when you're learning opponent patterns. Hitting early (as I did with Gamma in round 1) does not guarantee future hits; continue rotating positions rather than assuming a successful hit means the target will stay in that cell. The game punishes predictability more heavily than it rewards exploiting a single successful targeting.

# PICKET COLLUSION PLAYBOOK

## HIDING

When I choose where to hide, I avoid the center and edges. I pick positions in the 2-8 range, favoring mid-range cells that aren't immediately obvious. I vary my position across rounds so I'm not trapped in a pattern.

When I see an opponent has been missing me repeatedly, I do not assume they'll keep missing—I change my position for the next round. However, changing position is not enough if the opponent is systematically targeting me; I need to move unpredictably and away from cells I've used recently.

After being hit, I treat that opponent as an active threat and prioritize evasion in subsequent rounds. A single hit is evidence of targeting, not chance.

## FIRING

When my standing order tells me to fire at a station, I fire at that station. I do not need to vary my fire position unpredictably; I should instead develop a strategy to exploit patterns in where opponents hide.

When I fire at a target repeatedly and miss every time, I should change my approach. Firing the same cell repeatedly against a moving opponent yields no information and wastes rounds. After a miss, consider whether my target is likely to return to that cell or avoid it.

I should track opponent fire patterns over multiple rounds to infer their likely hiding positions, not assume they use the same cell twice.

## CLAIMING

When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I claim that result accurately. I do not lie on claims; the office verifies them and lying damages my credibility with no gain.

## ESCORT CLAIMS

When asked to name an escort, I only name a boat if I have reason to believe that boat will name me back. Otherwise I claim none.

I watch for patterns in which boats coordinate with each other, and I attempt to reciprocate those escort bonds when possible.

An escort claim is only worth 5 points if mutual. If I am not being escorted back by any boat, claiming an escort that won't reciprocate is a pure loss. In this game, mutual escort appears rare—I should not force an escort claim without evidence of reciprocal intent.

## GENERAL STRATEGY

I prioritize accurate claims and honesty. A strong scoring position is worth more than short-term gains from deception.

I pay attention to who is firing at whom each round and adjust my hiding position accordingly.

I exploit the standing firing order: if I can land consistent hits on my assigned target while opponents miss me, I build a lead over time.

However, consistency in firing position against a mobile opponent is a liability. After missing the same target at the same cell multiple rounds in a row, I should shift my firing cell to force my target into an unfamiliar evasion problem.

I should expect that some opponents will not reciprocate escort coordination. Unilateral escort claims are losses; I should remain cautious about naming escorts unless I have observed clear evidence of mutual coordination.
